chapters.title: Email, explained
chapters.intro:
How email actually works, why mail servers are so easy to get wrong, what fifty years of fixes have solved, and what is still broken. Written for anyone who has tried to run a mail server, or wondered why it is so hard.

It is the guide we wished we had when we were learning. It is written to be useful whatever server you run; REST Mail's own approach comes last in each chapter, after the problem and the standard fixes, never instead of them.

sections.title: How to read it
sections.html:
Each chapter follows the same pattern:

  1. The problem. What goes wrong without this, in plain words.
  2. How it works. The protocol or setting, with a diagram.
  3. What goes wrong. The common mistakes, and why they are easy to make.
  4. How REST Mail handles it. With links to the code that does it.
  5. Sources. The RFCs and documentation every claim comes from.

These files are the source of truth. The guide on rest-mail.com is built from them, with the diagrams made interactive, so the two never drift apart. How that build works is being designed in docs/design/email-explained-website.md.

sections.title: Contents
sections.html:
Chapters with a link are written. The rest are planned.

Part 1: How email works

  • The journey of a message: from your mail app to someone else's inbox, hop by hop
  • DNS for email: MX, A and AAAA, reverse DNS, null MX
  • SMTP as a conversation: EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, and the reply codes
  • The message itself: headers, MIME, encodings, envelope versus header
  • Bounces, queues and retries: delivery status notifications, deferral, backscatter
  • Reading mail: POP3, IMAP, JMAP, Sieve and ManageSieve
  • Finding the server: autoconfig, Autodiscover and SRV records

Part 2: The security layers, one at a time

  • Encryption in transit: STARTTLS versus implicit TLS, and downgrade attacks
  • MTA-STS, TLS-RPT, DANE and DNSSEC
  • Who may send: SMTP AUTH, SASL, app passwords, and why submission needs a login
  • SPF: who may send for a domain, the 10-lookup limit, and why forwarding breaks it
  • DKIM: signatures, selectors, key rotation, and what breaks them
  • DMARC: alignment, policies, reports, and p=reject versus forwarding
  • ARC: authentication that survives forwarding
  • Spam defences: blocklists, greylisting, rate limits, content scanning, reputation
  • Bulk mail: List-Unsubscribe, one-click unsubscribe, and the 2024 sender rules

Part 3: How it goes wrong

  • The open relay and the spam machine
  • The black hole: how mail is silently lost
  • Why the security layers are so hard to get right
  • Deliverability: reputation, warm-up, and why big providers distrust small servers

Part 4: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits

  • The servers compared: Postfix, Exim, Sendmail, OpenSMTPD, Dovecot, Stalwart, Maddy, Haraka, and the paid, proprietary services (Microsoft Exchange and Microsoft 365, Google Workspace)
  • Containers and bundles: what packaging solves, and what stays the same. How docker-mailserver, mailcow, Mailu, Mail-in-a-Box, iRedMail and kubernetes-mail-server package Postfix, Dovecot and the rest, what that makes easier, and what is still inside. REST Mail's author built kubernetes-mail-server, and a Docker-based server before it; this chapter draws on that experience
  • Efforts to modernise email: JMAP and others, what each solves, where each stands today, and how they relate to REST Mail
  • What REST Mail does differently
  • RESTMAIL: delivery between servers over HTTPS
  • Migrating step by step, without breaking anything
  • Solved, solving, still open

Reference

  • Glossary
  • Check your own server: a checklist

chapters.title: The open relay and the spam machine
chapters.summary: How a mail server ends up sending strangers' spam, the four mistakes behind it, what it costs, and how to check your own.
chapters.intro:
A mail server has to do two things that pull against each other. It must accept mail from anyone on the internet, because that is how mail for your domain arrives. And it must refuse to pass mail on to anyone else, unless the sender is one of your own users. Get the first half wrong and your users miss mail. Get the second half wrong and strangers use your server to send their spam.

There are two ways to get it wrong:

  • An open relay delivers mail for anyone who connects. No password needed.
  • A spam machine delivers mail for one stolen login, as fast as it can.

Either way, the spam leaves from your server's address, and the rest of the internet holds you responsible for it.

The diagram's source is open-relay.workflow.json. On the website it is interactive: it animates, and you can follow any path through it.

sections.title: How common is it?
sections.html:
Stolen logins are a long-running, current problem. In 2012 Spamhaus wrote that spam sent "through compromised user accounts on legitimate mail servers that use SMTP AUTH authentication" had "grown precipitously" and was "a major vector for criminal spam" (Spamhaus, 2012). In 2024 it wrote that "the problem of spam through hacked accounts has been plaguing the internet for years", and it keeps a dedicated list, AuthBL, of addresses "known to host bots using brute force or stolen SMTP AUTH credentials to send spam, phishing and malware emails" (Spamhaus, 2024).

Open relays are rarer than they were, because modern servers refuse to relay by default. Each of the mistakes below brings one back. We have not found a current, reliable count of open relays on the internet. If you know of one, please open an issue.

sections.title: The rule every server has to get right
sections.titleHtml: The rule every server has to get right
sections.html:
When a client sends RCPT TO:<someone@example.org>, the server asks one question: is this recipient mine?

  • Yes, the domain is one this server hosts: accept it. This is mail arriving for your users, and it may come from anyone.
  • No, the domain belongs to someone else: accept it only from a client you trust, or from one of your users who has signed in. Otherwise refuse.

Passing mail on to another server is called relaying. A server that relays for anyone is an open relay. The internet's mail standards have asked servers not to do this since 1999 (RFC 2505).

Postfix answers the question with a restriction list, evaluated for every RCPT TO. Its default, since Postfix 2.10, is:

smtpd_relay_restrictions = permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, defer_unauth_destination

Read it left to right:

  1. permit_mynetworks: if the client's IP address is in mynetworks, accept.
  2. permit_sasl_authenticated: if the client signed in, accept.
  3. defer_unauth_destination: if the recipient is not ours, refuse.

The first rule that matches decides. A permit ends the list, and nothing after it runs. That one fact is behind most of what follows.

Postfix has a safety net: it refuses to receive mail at all unless one of its restriction lists contains a rejecting rule, such as reject_unauth_destination or defer_unauth_destination (postconf: smtpd_relay_restrictions). The net checks that a rejecting rule exists. It cannot check that a permit placed before it will never match a stranger.

sections.title: Four ways tutorials break it
sections.html:
Most self-hosted mail servers are assembled from tutorials. Each one copies a different set of lines, often written for an older Postfix, and each fixes the problem in front of it. These four mistakes come up again and again.

1. mynetworks that trusts too much

permit_mynetworks exists so that machines on your own network can send without signing in. A typical story: an application on another server cannot send mail, a guide says to add its network to mynetworks, and the quickest change that works is:

mynetworks = 0.0.0.0/0

That trusts every IPv4 address on the internet. Wider-than-intended ranges do the same thing more quietly: a whole cloud provider's private range, or mynetworks_style = class, which Postfix itself warns "may cause Postfix to 'trust' your entire provider's network" (postconf: mynetworks_style).

The default is safe in modern Postfix: since 3.0, mynetworks_style defaults to host, trusting only the machine itself. But only at compatibility_level = 2 or higher. A server upgraded from an older release often keeps a lower level, and with it the old subnet default, which trusts every machine on the same network (COMPATIBILITY_README).

2. A gateway that makes every client look local

permit_mynetworks judges a client by its IP address. When something forwards connections to Postfix, Postfix can see the forwarder's address instead of the real client's:

  • Docker with IPv6: an IPv6 connection to a container that only has an IPv4 address is forwarded by Docker's userland proxy, and arrives from the network's gateway address (for example 172.17.0.1). docker-mailserver warns that trusting the Docker network "can create an open relay, for instance if IPv6 is enabled on the host machine" (docker-mailserver: PERMIT_DOCKER, IPv6).
  • A TCP proxy or load balancer in front of Postfix, without the PROXY protocol, makes every connection come from the proxy.
  • Kubernetes services do the same by default: with the default externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster, "the source IP seen in the target container is not the original source IP of the client" (Kubernetes: preserving the client source IP).

Tutorials for containers often add the container network to mynetworks, so that other containers can send mail. Combine that with any of the above, and everyone on the internet arrives looking like a trusted local machine.

The fix is to give Postfix the real address, with smtpd_upstream_proxy_protocol = haproxy behind a proxy (postconf), and never to trust a gateway's address.

3. A permit before the reject

Before Postfix 2.10, relay control and spam filtering shared one list, smtpd_recipient_restrictions, which Postfix's own documentation calls "error-prone configuration" (postconf: smtpd_relay_restrictions). Any permit placed before reject_unauth_destination lets a stranger through.

Postfix's documentation gives a real example (SMTPD_ACCESS_README):

smtpd_recipient_restrictions =
    permit_mynetworks
    check_helo_access hash:/etc/postfix/helo_access
    reject_unknown_helo_hostname
    reject_unauth_destination

# /etc/postfix/helo_access
localhost.localdomain PERMIT

The exception was meant for one machine that greets with HELO localhost.localdomain. But anyone can send that greeting, and in their words this makes Postfix "an open relay for all such hosts".

Postfix 2.10 separated the two lists, so this can no longer happen by accident. But for servers migrating from older versions, the documentation allows setting smtpd_relay_restrictions empty and using smtpd_recipient_restrictions "exactly as before". Tutorials that copy that line bring the old trap back.

4. A stolen password and no limits

permit_sasl_authenticated is correct: your users sign in and send. The trouble starts when a password leaks, through phishing, reuse or guessing. From then on, a spammer is one of your users.

Postfix does not limit how much a signed-in user sends. Its rate limits are per client address, and off by default: smtpd_client_message_rate_limit defaults to 0, meaning "a client can send as many message delivery requests per time unit as Postfix can accept" (postconf). A spammer spreading over many addresses is not slowed at all. Limiting per account needs a separate policy service, which most tutorials leave out.

sections.title: Why age makes it worse
sections.html:
None of these mistakes is a bug in Postfix. Postfix is carefully built and well documented. The trouble is that every safer default had to be added on top of older behaviour, without breaking the servers already running it:

  • Safer defaults arrive behind a switch. mynetworks_style = host is the default only at compatibility_level = 2 or higher. An upgraded server keeps the older, wider default until someone raises the level by hand (COMPATIBILITY_README).
  • The old shape stays supported. Setting smtpd_relay_restrictions empty brings back the pre-2.10 combined list, "exactly as before" (postconf).
  • Tutorials outlive the versions they were written for, and are copied into new servers years later.
  • Every protection added since (encryption, sign-in, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS) is another daemon or setting with its own syntax, each with mistakes of its own. Part 2 of this guide goes through them one at a time.

So a server can follow its documentation, start without a warning, and still relay for strangers. REST Mail starts from the other end. It is one modern stack in which the safe behaviour is the only behaviour. Compatibility lives at the edge, where it still speaks SMTP, IMAP and POP3 to everyone, not in a configuration file that carries every old default forward.

sections.title: What it costs
sections.html:
• Blocklists. Large mailbox providers and blocklist operators such as Spamhaus see spam from your address, and list it.
  • Your real mail bounces. Servers that check those lists refuse mail from your address, so your users' ordinary mail is rejected with 550 5.7.1 until you are delisted, which happens only after the server is cleaned up.
  • Your host steps in. Hosting providers block port 25 or suspend servers that send spam.
  • Backscatter. Spam sent with forged senders bounces back to those senders, innocent people who never sent anything (BACKSCATTER_README).

sections.title: How to check your own server
sections.titleHtml: How to check your own server
sections.html:
From a machine outside your network, try to relay through your server:

swaks --server mail.example.com --from test@example.net --to someone@gmail.com

A correct server refuses the recipient with 454 4.7.1 (the default defer_unauth_destination) or 554 5.7.1 (reject_unauth_destination), both with "Relay access denied". If it answers 250, it is an open relay.

On the server, read what is actually in effect:

postconf -n mynetworks mynetworks_style compatibility_level smtpd_relay_restrictions smtpd_recipient_restrictions

Check that mynetworks lists only addresses you control, that no permit comes before the rejecting rule, and that a growing queue (postqueue -p) is not your first sign of trouble.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
REST Mail removes the decision that goes wrong, rather than asking you to configure it correctly:

  • No trusted networks. On port 25, REST Mail accepts a recipient only if it is a mailbox it hosts; any other recipient is refused with 550 5.1.1, whatever the client's address. There is no mynetworks to widen. Repeated misses slow the client down. (internal/gateway/smtp/session.go, Rcpt)
  • Relaying only for users who signed in, on the submission port, 465, with TLS from the first byte. MAIL FROM without a login is refused with 530. (session.go, server.go)
  • A real address behind a proxy. REST Mail reads the client's address through the PROXY protocol, only from proxies listed as trusted. Even then, an address never grants relaying. (proxyproto.go)
  • Limits per account, on by default. Each signed-in account has a sending rate limit (451 4.7.1 when exceeded, #171), at most 100 recipients per message, and may only send from addresses it owns (550 otherwise). The REST API's send path has the same limits (#184). These are two of the defences Spamhaus recommends to every mail service: "default per-account limits on numbers of outgoing emails", and "disallowing sending from domains whose mail you do not host" (Spamhaus, 2024).

The trade-off: an application that wants to send through REST Mail signs in with an app password, instead of being trusted for its address.
